name: The Great Himalayas (Himadri)
description: Young fold mountains formed by the ongoing collision between the Indian and Eurasian tectonic plates. Spans ~2,400 km in an arcuate shape.
highestPeakInfo: Mount Everest (8,848.86 m - Nepal/Tibet border). Highest peak in India: Kangchenjunga (8,586 m, Sikkim). Highest peak entirely in India: Nanda Devi (7,816 m, Uttarakhand).
examFacts: Classified into three longitudinal parallel ranges: Greater Himalayas (Himadri, average elevation 6,000 m), Lesser Himalayas (Himachal / Middle Himalayas, 3,700-4,500 m), and Outer Himalayas (Shivaliks, 900-1,100 m).
Formed during the Tertiary period by the collision of the northward-drifting Indian Plate with the Eurasian Plate.
Source of major perennial antecedent river systems including the Indus, Ganga, and Brahmaputra.
Contains the world's highest non-polar glaciers including Siachen, Gangotri, and Baltoro.
Acts as an impenetrable climatic barrier blocking freezing Central Asian winds from entering India in winter and forcing the South-West Monsoon to shed precipitation over the subcontinent.

name: Western Ghats (Sahyadri)
description: A continuous escarpment spanning ~1,600 km parallel to the Arabian Sea coast, extending from Tapi valley to Kanyakumari. A global biodiversity hotspot.
highestPeakInfo: Anamudi (2,695 m, Eravikulam National Park, Kerala) - highest peak in Peninsular India.
examFacts: Recognized by UNESCO as a serial World Heritage Site (2012) and one of the world's eight 'hottest hotspots' of biological diversity.
Not true fold mountains but faulted escarpments of the Deccan plateau trap formed during the break-up of Gondwanaland.
Origin of major peninsular east-flowing rivers (Godavari, Krishna, Kaveri) and west-flowing perennial coastal rivers (Mandovi, Zuari, Sharavathi, Periyar).
Divided by major natural passes: Thal Ghat (Mumbai-Nashik), Bhor Ghat (Mumbai-Pune), and Palakkad Gap (between Nilgiris and Anaimalai, connecting Kerala to Tamil Nadu).
Western slopes receive heavy orographic rainfall exceeding 3,000–5,000 mm, leaving the interior Deccan in a pronounced rain shadow.

name: Eastern Ghats (Purva Ghat)
description: A discontinuous and dissected chain of relict mountains running parallel to the Bay of Bengal, heavily eroded by major eastward peninsular rivers.
highestPeakInfo: Arma Konda / Jindhagada Peak (1,690 m, Araku Valley, Visakhapatnam, Andhra Pradesh) and Deomali (1,672 m, Odisha).
examFacts: Older geologically than the Western Ghats, representing deeply eroded remnants of ancient fold belts.
Dissected into distinct regional hill tracts: Mahendragiri in Odisha, Nallamala, Erramala, and Seshachalam in Andhra Pradesh, and Javadi, Shevaroy, and Kalrayan in Tamil Nadu.
Meets the Western Ghats at the Nilgiri Hills in Tamil Nadu, forming a complex ecological junction.
Home to extensive bauxite plateaus (Panchpatmali, Niyamgiri) and red sanders (Pterocarpus santalinus) in the Seshachalam Biosphere Reserve.
Receives substantial precipitation during the North-East Retreating Monsoon (October–December).

name: Aravalli Range
description: One of the oldest geological fold mountain systems in the world, dating back to the Proterozoic eon. Runs ~692 km southwest-to-northeast from Himmatnagar (Gujarat) to Delhi.
highestPeakInfo: Guru Shikhar (1,722 m, Mount Abu, Sirohi district, Rajasthan).
examFacts: Recognized as a classic example of relict/residual fold mountains worn down by hundreds of millions of years of subaerial weathering.
Acts as a vital water divide between the Arabian Sea drainage (Luni, Sabarmati, Banas) and the Bay of Bengal drainage (Chambal, Yamuna).
Crucial ecological barrier preventing eastward expansion and desertification of the Thar Desert into the fertile Indo-Gangetic Plains.
The northernmost tip forms the Delhi Ridge, which terminates near the Yamuna River in New Delhi.
Hosts Mount Abu, Rajasthan's only hill station, featuring Nakki Lake and the exquisite marble Dilwara Jain Temples.

name: Vindhya Range
description: A broken chain of relict sandstone and limestone scarp hills running west to east across Central India, historically demarcating North India from the Deccan.
highestPeakInfo: Sadbhawna Shikhar / Kalumar Peak (752 m, Damoh district, Madhya Pradesh).
examFacts: Forms the northern boundary of the Narmada Rift Valley, composed primarily of Vindhyan sandstones and shales.
Historically considered the traditional dividing line between Aryavarta (North India) and Dakshinapatha (South India).
Extends eastward as the Bharner and Kaimur ranges into eastern Madhya Pradesh, southern Uttar Pradesh, and the Rohtas plateau in Bihar.
Renowned for sedimentary mineral resources including building stone, limestone for cement, and the diamond-bearing kimberlite pipes of Panna.
Birthplace of several northward tributaries of the Yamuna and Ganga including the Chambal, Betwa, and Ken.

name: Satpura Range
description: A series of seven folded and faulted ranges (Satpura = Seven Folds) running parallel between the Narmada and Tapi rift valleys.
highestPeakInfo: Dhupgarh (1,350 m, Mahadeo Hills near Pachmarhi, Hoshangabad, Madhya Pradesh).
examFacts: True horst mountain (block mountain) bounded by grabens: the Narmada rift valley to the north and the Tapi rift valley to the south.
Divisible into three sections: Rajpipla Hills in the west, Mahadeo Hills in the central part, and Maikal Hills in the east.
Amarkantak Plateau in the Maikal Range is a radial drainage hub where the Narmada, Son, and Johila rivers originate within close proximity.
Pachmarhi in the Mahadeo Hills is Madhya Pradesh's sole hill station and was designated a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve in 2009.
Hosts premier Project Tiger reserves including Kanha, Satpura, Pench, and Melghat.

name: Nilgiri Hills ('Blue Mountains')
description: A mountainous massif at the junction of the Western Ghats and Eastern Ghats, famous for tea plantations, shola-grassland ecosystems, and indigenous tribes.
highestPeakInfo: Doddabetta (2,637 m, Nilgiris district, Tamil Nadu) - second highest peak in Peninsular India.
examFacts: Nilgiri Biosphere Reserve was the very first Biosphere Reserve established in India under UNESCO's MAB programme (1986).
Home to endemic Shola forests (stunted montane evergreen forests nestled in undulating high-altitude rolling grasslands).
Traditional homeland of the Toda, Kota, Kurumba, Irula, and Badaga tribal communities.
Connected to the Mettupalayam plains via the Nilgiri Mountain Railway (UNESCO World Heritage Site), which utilizes the unique Abt rack-and-pinion system.
Habitat of the endangered Nilgiri Tahr (Nilgiritragus hylocrius) and the rare mass-flowering Neelakurinji (Strobilanthes kunthiana, blooming once every 12 years).

name: Thar Desert (The Great Indian Desert)
description: The world's ninth largest subtropical desert, spanning ~200,000 sq km. Characterized by undulating sand dunes (barchans, longitudinal dunes) and extreme diurnal temperatures.
examFacts: Most densely populated desert in the world, with an average human population density of ~83 persons per sq km compared to 5–10 in typical global deserts.
Transformed agriculturally by the Indira Gandhi Canal (Rajasthan Feeder), which brings water over 650 km from Harike Barrage on the Beas-Sutlej confluence to western Rajasthan.
Contains the Desert National Park (Jaisalmer-Barmer), the prime sanctuary for the critically endangered Great Indian Bustard (Godawan).
Bhadla Solar Park in the Phalodi/Jodhpur region is one of the world's largest operational solar power installations (~2,245 MW).
Contains ancient fossil evidence such as the Akal Wood Fossil Park (180-million-year-old Jurassic wood petrifications near Jaisalmer).

name: Deccan Plateau
description: Vast triangular volcanic plateau sloping gently eastwards, bounded by the Western Ghats to the west, Eastern Ghats to the east, and Satpura-Vindhya to the north.
examFacts: Formed by massive Cretaceous-Tertiary fissure eruptions of basaltic lava (~66 million years ago), creating step-like geological formations known as 'Deccan Traps'.
Deep weathering of basaltic rocks created rich Black Cotton Soils (Regur), characterized by high clay content, self-ploughing moisture retention, and suitability for cotton and sugarcane.
Drained by major eastward rivers: Godavari, Krishna, and Kaveri, creating deeply incised river valleys and fertile deltaic floodplains along the Bay of Bengal coast.
Mineral-rich plateau hosting gold (Hutti), iron ore (Ballari, Sandur), manganese, and limestone.
Historically the core territory of major empires: Satavahanas, Chalukyas, Rashtrakutas, Bahmanis, Vijayanagara, and Marathas.

name: Chota Nagpur Plateau
description: Mineral heartland of India ('Ruhr of India'), composed of ancient Archean granites and gneisses with Gondwana coal-bearing sedimentary formations.
examFacts: Contains over 40% of India's mineral reserves, including prime coking coal (Jharia, Bokaro), hematite iron ore (Noamundi, Singhbhum), uranium (Jaduguda), copper (Ghatsila), and mica (Koderma).
Drained radically by the Damodar, Subarnarekha, North Koel, South Koel, and Barakar rivers.
Damodar Valley Corporation (DVC), modeled on the US Tennessee Valley Authority (TVA) in 1948, was independent India's first multipurpose river valley project.
Composed of stepped erosion surfaces known as Patlands (e.g., Netarhat plateau, elevated at ~1,000 m).
Highest point is Parasnath Hill (Shikharji, 1,365 m), the supreme Jain pilgrimage shrine where 20 Tirthankaras attained Nirvana.
